In Fortran 90, they can be explicit-shape, or they can be made assumed-shape using the allocatable keyword. C creates them dynamically with malloc, while C++ and Java use the new command. For 10 points—name this programming construct, consisting of any data structure with multiple elements.

The eastern Koolau and western Waianae ranges divide it into the leeward, windward, and central sections. The Diamond Head crater lies located on its southeastern coast, while Kaneohe Bay is on its east. Kauai Channel separates it from the island of that name, and a trip south across Kaiwi Channel lands one on Molokai. Waipahu and Kailua are among its cities. For 10 points—name this most populous island of Hawaii, the location of Honolulu.

Filming in Spain, where the train-wreck scenes were shot, was halted for three months while screenwriter Robert Bolt was in jail for participating in an anti-nuclear demonstration. Director David Lean has a cameo as the voice of a motorcyclist shouting "Who are you?" across the Suez Canal. Katherine Hepburn helped convince Lean, when he couldn't get Albert Finney, to cast Peter O'Toole in the title role. For 10 points—name this 1962 World War I film.

Anthony Kennedy showed concern for the psychological pressures it creates in his majority opinion in Lee v. Weisman. In 2000, the Supreme Court ruled that the Santa Fe Independent School District in Texas could not allow it at high school football games. Often subject to a test established in Lemon v. Kurtzman, for 10 points—what is this practice that Engel v. Vitale ruled unconstitutional at institutions of public education?

Richard Henry Dana considered it a hoax and wrote, "No one, on this side of the Atlantic, is capable of writing such verses." In a bleak tone, this poem notes "All that breathe / Will share thy destiny," and that "Earth, that nourished thee, shall claim / Thy growth." Another line states "Yet not to thine eternal resting-place/Shalt thou retire alone," and the poem begins with the line "To him who in the love of nature holds/Communion with her visible forms." For 10 points—name this poem by William Cullen Bryant.

His coronation was overshadowed by a catastrophe where over a thousand spectators were crushed to death. Married to Alix of Hessen, his reign was marked by two futile wars, the Bloody Sunday massacre of 1905, and the October Manifesto which established a Duma dominated by his minister, Peter Stolypin. For 10 points—name this person killed at Yekaterinburg with his family in 1917, the last tsar of Russia.

After marrying Jetta Umiker, he moved to Rome where he painted the realistic landscape Atrani. After visiting the Alhambra, he became captivated by Moorish ornamentation and by visual depiction of mathematical concepts; he later created Ascending and Descending, the Transformation prints, and Reptiles. For 10 points—name this graphic artist whose works involve "mental imagery" of repeated patterns and paradoxical constructions.

Its decline began in the 1390s, when it lost the battles of Kondurcha and Terek to Tamerlane. Earlier, it expanded into Poland and Hungary by defeating the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Liegnitz. Uzbeg converted it to Islam, less than a century after Batu established it. From its capital at Sarai Berke, it exacted regular tribute in a suzerainity arrangement. For 10 points—name this Mongol state which annihilated Moscow and Kiev to establish control over Russia.

In joining the Provisional Government, Fyodor Dan and Irakli Tsereteli ignored the advice of this group's leader, Julius Martov. Formed by Grigory Plekhanov in London in 1903, they believed that a liberal, capitalist regime must be put into place before socialism could arise, and they opposed limiting party membership to "professional revolutionaries." For 10 points—name this faction, with a name meaning "one of the minority," which opposed the Bolsheviks.

The link between it and the state of the hippocampus was determined when a patient known as H.M. Experienced complications after having most of his hippocampus surgically removed to stop epileptic seizures. Often linked to Korsakoff's syndrome and other sources of frontal lobe damage, for 10 points—what is this condition that comes in anterograde and retrograde varieties, a severe loss of memory?

The poet makes a reference to a bronze statue of Neptune at the end of this poem. The center of the work is a painting of the eponymous figure by Fra Pandolf. The speaker laments that her heart was "too easily impressed" by a "bough of cherries" and not enough by the "gift of a nine-hundred-years- old name." For 10 points—name this 1842 poem in which the speaker, the Duke of Ferrera, speaks glowingly of his former wife in a dramatic monologue by Robert Browning.

In this city, restaurant owner John Hickenlooper defeated City Auditor Don Mares, a favorite of the growing Latino community, in the race to succeed mayor Wellington Webb. Webb replaced Federico Pena when the latter joined the Clinton administration. Issues include a proposed public smoking ban, construction on Interstate 25, and the water quality in the South Platte River. For 10 points—name this large state capital in the Rockies.

His law of phosphorescence states if a solid is capable of absorbing light it may re-emit light. His law of terminal speed states that the viscous drag force experienced by a sphere moving through a fluid is 6 pi times the product of the radius of the sphere, the speed of the sphere and the fluid's viscocity. For 10 points—name this Scottish physicist better known to calculus students for his theorem that relates line integrals of vector fields to surface integrals of vector fields.

At the Battle of Ticinus, he mounted a horse and charged the Roman troops about to encircle his fallen father. This act of courage earned this then-eighteen-year-old the corona civica, the highest Roman military citation, but he refused. Later, he defeated Gisco at Great Plains and went on to conquer another foe at Ilipa and Baecula. For 10 points—name this victor at Zama, the Roman rival of Hannibal in the Second Punic War.

Gaspar Vargas and his son Sylvestre are both considered primary influences upon this genre of music. Most ensembles usually perform renditions of Cielito Lindo and Jalisco, with characteristic gritos interspersed. For 10 points—name this band of four to nine musicians who perform songs from the heritage of Mexico, usually while wearing sombreros.

After studying under Robert Lowell in 1959, this author wrote the poems published as The Colossus, Crossing the Water, and Winter Trees. Her famous works include "Daddy," "Lady Lazarus," and "Edge," which has been dated to a week before her death. Using the pseudonym Victoria Lucas, she published her only novel the same year she died by putting her head in an oven. For 10 points—name this wife of Ted Hughes and author of The Bell Jar.

It first appeared in a 1917 collection entitled Saltbush Bill, J.P., and Other Verses. This poem describes a hobo who drowns himself after being accosted by a Trooper inquiring about the jumbuck in a Tucker bag. It starts when a jolly swagman sits beside a billabong under the shade of a coolibah tree. For 10 points—name this unofficial national anthem of Australia.

Directed by Robert Fechner, it paid twenty-five dollars a month to three million recipients. Its projects included planting trees, building flood barriers, laying telephone lines, fighting forest fires, and maintaining forest roads and trails. For 10 points—name this "makework" agency of the New Deal.

From his early works in Russia to landscapes he created in Munich during the 1910's, many of his paintings feature a horse-and-rider motif that symbolized his defiance of the conservative aesthetic values of the Neue Kunstlervereinigung (KOONST-ler-vair-AYE-ni-gung). The motif also appeared on the cover of his manifesto, On the Spiritual in Art. For 10 points—name this painter of the Composition and Impression series who joined with Franz Marc to found Der Blau Reiter.

His ship, Hringhorn, was the largest in the world, and upon his death it was set afire and pushed into the sea bearing his body and the body of his wife, Nanna, who died of a broken heart. After he died, Hel offered to resurrect him if every creature on earth mourned for him, though this effort failed because Loki disguised himself as a giantess and refused to mourn. For 10 points—name this Norse god who was killed when his blind brother Hodur hit him with a dart made of mistletoe.

It was formed by four Philadelphia Press staffers who later created the Society of Independent Artists. This group had no particular program but was held together by a common opposition to academicism, as seen in the works of Arthur B. Davies, Maurice Prendergast, Ernest Lawson, and John Sloan, which depicted urban life realistically. For 10 points—name this group, also called "the eight," led by Robert Henri.

It was conceived by John McConnell, who persuaded the San Francisco Board of Supervisors to pass a resolution in observance of it. It was first celebrated by the United Nations on March 21, 1971, with the ringing of the Peace Bell at the moment of the vernal equinox. That same year, Senator Gaylord Nelson declared a week-long celebration in April. For 10 points—name this environmental holiday.

In September 2002, he defeated Edmund Stoiber of the Conservative Social Union to retain his job. Since then, he has had to apologize for comments made by Joschka Fischer, his foreign minister, who took this man's own anti-war line to extremes by calling George W. Bush "Adolf Nazi." For 10 points—name this leader of the Social Democrats and Chancellor of Germany.

After he deposed the powerful Praetorian Guard commander Perennis for conspiring against him, he installed Cleander, whose corruption outraged the people to riot. He banished his wife Crispina for another conspiracy and executed his sister Lucilla for a third. Coins and busts of him often depict him with a club and a lion skin wrapped around his shoulders, for he thought himself a reincarnation of Hercules. For 10 points—name this successor of Marcus Aurelius who actually was killed in a gladiatorial fight.

Tom grows up at Offal Court, where his drunken father punishes him whenever he comes home empty after a day of begging on the streets. When opportunity presents itself, he pardons the Duke of Norfolk and many prisoners to the adulation of the public. He is just about to be crowned when Edward storms in and declares his identity. For 10 points—name this story about switching places between social classes by Mark Twain.

The narrator laments, "I should have been a pair of ragged claws / Scuttling across the floors of silent seas." Earlier, he comments he has "known the arms already, / known them all – / Arms that are braceleted and white and bare." Later in this poem, the narrator and title character asserts he is "not Prince Hamlet, nor was meant to be", and asks "Do I dare / Disturb the universe?" Beginning with the line "Let us go then, you and I," for 10 points—identify this poem by T. S. Eliot about the women coming and going and talking of Michelangelo.

He angered many by making his lover George Villiers the Earl of Buckingham. Despite his affair with Villiers, he had eight children with Anne of Denmark, but only three survived past the age of two. A prolific author, he wrote a treatise against the use of tobacco and a defense of the divine right of kings. For 10 points—name this son of Mary Queen of Scots and father of Charles I, the first Stuart king of England and the patron of a namesake translation of the Bible.

Though he was known by the name of Kinsaku while working in the service of Todo Yoshitada, he changed his name in the 1680s to that of his home, the "Cottage of the Plantain Tree." A traveler for much of his life, he penned the travelogues The Records of a Travel Worn Satchel and The Narrow Road to the Deep North. For 10 points—name this Japanese author, the developer and master of haiku.

The first play in this trilogy details the murder of the title character and his slave Cassandra by his treacherous wife and her lover Aegisthus. The second play shows the vengeance wrought by Agamemmnon's son against Clytemnestra. The son is promptly chased to Athens by the title characters of the third play, where he is absolved by Athena and the Areopagus. For 10 points—Agamemmnon, The Libation Bearers and The Eumenides make up what trilogy by Aeschylus?

Patients treated with penicillin often exhibit the Jarisch- Herxheimer reaction, which is an immediate general worsening of symptoms like anxiety, malaise, and exacerbated lesions. Caused by the spirochete Treponema palladium, some believe it was transmitted to European colonists by long- immune Native Americans. For 10 points—name this sexually-transmitted disease that was investigated in the infamous Tuskegee Study.

Because Grant chose to drill his men rather than fortify the positions here, the Army of the Mississippi initially routed several units. However, reinforcements from Don Carlos Buell's Army of the Ohio and the mortal wounding of Albert Sidney Johnston, which forced P.T. Beauregard to take full command mid-battle, spelled defeat for the southern forces. For 10 points—name this battle of April 6th and 7th, 1862, in Tennessee.

Among the varieties of this animal species are Tatersall's Sifaka, a particularly acrobatic and colorful version, the much larger indri, the avahi, and the hairy-eared pygmy variety. A research center at Duke University examines these slim-bodied prosimians related to the loris and the potto. For 10 points—what are these primates, living mainly on the island of Madagascar?

Followers believe that every living thing has a soul, or jiva, and that it can be freed from the body to live in eternal bliss by avoiding worldly pursuits. The holy sadhus and sadhvis try to live ideal lives, refraining from killing any living thing, holding almost no property, and begging for food. Divisions include the "white clad" and naked or "sky clad." For 10 points—name this religion founded by Mahavira.

Under the Cournot model of this structure, firms simultaneously determine their output, while under the Bertrand model firms make simultaneous decisions about price. Real world examples include the automobile industry for differentiated products and the steel and oil industries for non- differentiated products. For 10 points—name this market system where the production and distribution of a good is dominated by a few large firms.

In his 1898 speech to the Chicago Peace Jubilee, "Imperialism: Its Dangers and Wrongs," he denounced the "hordes of savage races" about to enter the U.S. Via annexed territory. After attending an 1879 lecture from the Christian socialist Thomas Hughes, he began using peaceful pressure tactics, although he went to prison in 1908 for violating an anti-boycott order during his feud with Buck's Stove and Range Company. For 10 points—name this New York cigar maker who founded the American Federation of Labor.

Preceded by the Taft-Katsura armistice, news of it caused the Hibiya Riot. Article III called for a simultaneous evacuation of Manchuria with the exception of the Liaodong Peninsula, which contained the cities of Talien and Port Arthur. Article IX gave the winner Sakhalin island, while Article XI transferred fishing rights in the Sea of Okhotsk. For 10 points—name this treaty, signed in New Hampshire, which earned Theodore Roosevelt the 1906 Nobel Peace prize for ending the Russo-Japanese War.

It ended in 1085 BCE when Smendes began a rival government at Tanis following the establishment of theocracy at Thebes and the death of Ramses XI. It began with the accession of Ahmose I and included the battles of Meggido and Kadesh, the reigns of Thutmose III, Akhenaton, and Hatsepshut, and the establishment of the Valley of the Kings. For 10 points—name this period including the eighteenth through twentieth Egyptian dynasties.

He died when the daughters of King Cocalus poured boiling water over him as he was bathing. The son of Zeus and Europa, he had the help of Poseidon in gaining control over the Aegean Islands, but after he failed to sacrifice a bull, Poseidon took revenge by implanting an "unnatural passion" in his daughter Phaedra. For 10 points—name this ruler of Crete who sacrificed Athenian youths to the resultant Minotaur.

He became executive of Baltimore County in 1962 on a graduated-tax platform and was elected governor of Maryland five years later. Fond of alliteration, his speeches denounced "pusillanimous pussyfooting" and "the nattering nabobs of negativism." For 10 points—name this man who, after pleading no contest to accepting bribes, resigned from his position as Richard Nixon's first Vice-President.

He disliked being called an existentialist, and he often coined new terms such as "dasein" in his works, making his prose somewhat difficulty to read. Although he had a lengthy affair with anti-Nazi Hannah Arendt, he had to retire from Freiburg after World War II because of his support for Hitler's regime. For 10 points—name this author of Being and Time.

Its chief justice was John Nash and its governor was William B. Ide. It began on June 14 with the seizure of Sonoma and the hasty painting of the namesake object by William Todd, a nephew of Lincoln. Taking advantage of the Mexican-American War, it existed for only a few months in 1846 under the de facto leadership of John C. Fremont. For 10 points—name this country in present-day California.

A national park since 1986, it boasts such varied scenery as the summit of Wheeler Peak, the sagebrush of its alluvial base, and the depths of the Lehman Caves. It is bordered by the Sierra Nevada on the west, the Columbia Plateau on the north, the Rockies on the northeast, the Colorado Plateau on the east, and the Mojave Desert on the south. For 10 points—name this topographic feature covering parts of six states and containing Death Valley.

The last Comanche chief, Quanah Parker, was allegedly cured of illness by ingesting a tea made from this, and he introduced it to numerous tribes in Oklahoma. In 1990's Employment Division v. Smith, the Supreme Court ruled that Oregon state laws prohibiting its use did not violate First Amendment rights to religion freedom. For 10 points—name this hallucinogenic drug that contains mescaline and comes from a cactus.

He is buried under a willow tree which he planted from a cutting taken at the tomb of Napoleon. He remained in his Senate seat after Tennessee seceeded, leading the War Democrats, and he became military governor of Tennessee before he was nominated as Vice-President. For 10 points—name this unpopular President whose violation of the Tenure of Office Act sparked his impeachment.

According to Ovid, she said, "Why should Latona be honored with worship, and none be paid to me? My father was Tantalus … My husband built and rules this city, Thebes, and Phrygia is my paternal inheritance. … Will you prefer to me this Latona, the Titan's daughter, with her two children? I have seven times as many." For 10 points—name this queen of Thebes whose husband Amphion and children were killed by Apollo and Diana for her boasting.

Contemporary legend held that they were descended from the rulers of Atlantis or an affair between Jesus and Mary Magdalene. Noted for their long hair, they were founded by a Salian who fought Attila the Hun alongside the Romans, Clovis I. For 10 points—name this dynasty which reunited the Frankish lands under Clothar II and was succeeded by the Carolingians.

Used as early as the Battle of Ma-Ling in China in 341 BCE, this weapon was known as an arbalest when the Normans introduced it to England. In 1139, the Second Lateran Council forbade its use against Christians, though it proved critical in the Crusader victory at Jaffa. For 10 points—name this ballistic weapon with a wooden stock in which the user triggered the release of an arrow.

He was conceived by a ray of light hitting the virgin Dughdova, and when he was born, he laughed. After reaching age 30, he received many revelations from the Holy Immortals and was thus able to resist the temptations of Ahriman. For 10 points—name this religious leader who wrote the Avesta to explain his Persian monotheistic faith.

It was expected he would become a rabbi like his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; but the death of his father before entering college eventually made him more secular. The founder of the first social science scholarly journal in France, the death of his son Andre in 1916 was devastating. The uncle of fellow sociologist Marcel MAuss, his works include The Division of Labor in Society. For 10 points—name this creator of the concept of "anomie" and author of the study Le Suicide.

Its authentic feeling results from the stay of the author, a great niece of Harriet Beecher Stowe, in the sanatorium of Dr. S. Weir Mitchell. The narrator is confined to her bedroom in a summer house as part of the rest cure for her "nervousness." The narrator's husband John insists that she remain completely inactive, not even picking up a pen to write. For 10 points—name this short story by Charlotte Perkins Gilman.

The original namesake of modern Cologne, she was killed at Antium after opposing the marriage of Poppaea Sabina and favoring her younger son Britannicus. She first married Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, while her third husband was Emperor Claudius, whom she may have fed poisoned mushrooms in her plot to put her son on the throne. For 10 points—name this sister of Caligula and mother and victim of Nero.

The names given to the four rooms inside of it were Camp Unity, Las Vegas Area, Heartbreak Hotel, and New Guy Village. Though in its native language it is named Hoa Lu, meaning "portable earthen stove," the French soldiers who built it in 1901 named it "rue de la Prison." For 10 points—name this complex which, from August 1964 to March 1973, house U.S. POWs in the North Vietnamese capital.

At its narrowest point, it is only fifty-five miles wide between Cape Dezhnyov and Cape Prince of Wales. Parts are as shallow as one hundred feet, and during the winter, ice fields cover its entirety, connecting the Diomede Islands to the Chukchi and Seward Peninsulas. For 10 points—name this waterway which separates Alaska and Siberia and may have been the entryway for Native American immigration.

It was first observed in 1899 during the autodecomposition of diazomethane in ether. Karl Ziegler won the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for synthesizing a high-density linear version of this material. The low-density variety is produced at pressures of 350 megapascals in the presence of peroxide initiators, leading to a partly crystalline material. For 10 points—what compound used in agricultural mulch, grocery bags, and milk bottles is the simplest and most ubiquitous of polymers?

After returning from exile in New Orleans, he began to travel in his trademark black carriage. He oversaw the writing of the Plan of Ayutla which outlined the principles of the rebellion against Santa Anna. As minister of justice under Igancio Comonfort, he issued a namesake law which restricted the roles of the church and army in government. He fled Mexico City in 1858 to establish a rival government at Veracruz. For 10 points—name this man who was president of Mexico before and after the empire of Maximillian.

Isle au Haut, one of the more than one thousand islands off this state's coast, sits at the entrance to Penobscot Bay. The bay's namesake river flows from Chamberlain Lake, while Moosehead Lake is the source of the Kennebeck. Cities include Caribou, Millinocket, Waterville, Auburn, Lewiston, and Bangor. For 10 points—name this state at the extreme northeast of the U.S.

Held at George Mann's Tavern, this meeting was convened to discuss problems in maritime commerce. Chairman John Dickinson found the task difficult with only five states sending delegations, so the topic turned to the creation of a more effective national government. For 10 points—name this September 1786 convention that concluded with a call to meet in Philadelphia the following year to amend the Articles of Confederation.

In 1930, he won the Harmon gold medal for literature for the novel Not Without Laughter. He worked as a sailor and a waiter, slipping poems onto Vachel Lindsay's plate in the latter job to get his break. While he also wrote popular plays such as Mulatto, he is probably best known for poetry collections such as Shakespeare in Harlem and The Weary Blues. For 10 points—name this Harlem Renaissance poet.

In response to his 1875 painting subtitled The Falling Rocket, John Ruskin called this artist a "coxcomb" who was "flinging a pot of paint in the public's face." He won a libel suit against Ruskin for one farthing, explaining during the trial why he called many of his paintings "nocturnes" or "symphonies." For 10 points—name this painter of Arrangement in Black and Grey: Portrait of the Painter's Mother.

An agreement in 638 between the Muslim caliph Omar ibn al-Khattab and the patriarch of the Greek Orthodox church made the Nuseibeh family the custodians of this site. First built in 335 by Constantine over the former site of a temple to Venus, it was rebuilt by Crusaders in 1099 around the rock believed to be Golgotha. For 10 points—identify this Jerusalem church which marks the place that Christians believe is the empty tomb of Jesus.

As part of his effort to popularize music, he founded the Festival of Two Worlds at Spoleto. He wrote his first opera, The Death of Pierrot, as a teenager, following that with the ballet Sebastian, the short operas The Medium and The Telephone, and his first full-length work, The Consul. In addition to writing original works, he was a librettist for other composers, writing for Samuel Barber's Vanessa. For 10 points—name this Italian-American composer of Amelia Goes to the Ball and Amahl and the Night Visitors.

The Store Baeljt Bridge links the city to the mainland, and its inner harbor divides Sjaelland and Amager islands. The city hall and the Church of Our Lady sit along Amailienbourg Square. Christiansborg Palace sits on the island of Slotsholmen, and near Langelinie Promenade sits an oft- beheaded statue. For 10 points—name this home of Tivoli Gardens, the Little Mermaid, and the governmental apparatus of Denmark.

Though eventually a devoted mother, she was known earlier in her life for her open liaisons with such figures as Jules Sandeau and Alfred Musset. Her novels, including The Haunted Pool, Fanchon the Cricket, A Winter in Majorca, and Indiana, are marked by moral idealism and a respect for nature. For 10 points—name this woman, born Aurore Dupin, who had a lengthy affair with Frederic Chopin.

They are the causative agent of URE-3, which kills yeast cells by reducing their nitrogen intake. Stemming from the PrP protein in mammals, they can "cluster," forming randomly distributed amyloid fibers which resemble those found in Alzheimer's patients. They were first hypothesized by Stanley Prusiner to explain scrapie in sheep. For 10 points—name these self- replicating infectious proteins which cause kuru, Creutzfeld-Jakob (YAH-kub) syndrome, and mad cow disease.

Initially supporting Mussolini, he gave his 1934 Nobel medal to the Italian government to be melted down for use against Abyssinia, but he later expressed his worries about fascism in The Mountain Giants. In his play Tonight We Improvise, the action takes place entirely within the audience, and his wife's insanity inspired Henry IV. For 10 points—name this Italian playwright who wrote of a confused family of actors wandering into the wrong play in Six Characters in Search of an Author.

By 1833, only two years after its founding in Marseille, it had over fifty thousand members, and Austria declared participation in it treason punishable by death. Parallel organizations later arose in Poland and Germany and were linked to it by its founder's 1834 attempt to turn it into a pan- European movement. For 10 points—name this group which attempted to seize Sardinia in 1833, created as a replacement for the Carbonari by Giuseppe Mazzini.

As a painter, he created the altarpiece at Paumgärtner and an imitation of Bellini, Feast of the Rose-Garlands. As an engraver, his works include St. Jerome in His Study and Melancholia I. As an instructive writer, he penned Treatise on Measurement and Four Books on Human Proportions. However, he is likely most associated with another medium in which he portrayed the Great Passion, Life of the Virgin, and the four horsemen of the Apocalypse. For 10 points—name this German master of woodcuts.

He protected the innocent from the jaws of Ammut but allowed her to devour the guilty. When Osiris died, he embalmed the body and wrapped it in a linen cloth to prevent decay, thus inventing the process of mummification. For 10 points—name this Egyptian god who weighed the hearts of the dead and led them to the afterlife, often depicted with the head of a jackal.

Its founders included John Lester, James Crowe, John D. Kennedy, and Frank McCord. In 1915, William J. Simmons revived it. The case of Bradenburg v. Ohio ruled that its members had the right to advocate violence as a means of effecting political change. Famous members included Harry Truman, Hugo Black, Robert Byrd, David Duke, and Nathan Bedford Forrest. For 10 points—name this white supremacist organization known for burning crosses.

Premiering in October 1942 with a performance by the Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo, its songs include "Saturday Night Waltz," "Buckaroo Holiday," and "Hoedown." Subtitled "The Courting at Burnt Ranch," it was choreographed by Agnes de Mille, who starred in its first performances. For 10 points—name this ballet with music by Aaron Copland, a love story set in the American Southwest.

He succeeded his father, Omar Sheik, as king of Ferghana at the age of twelve. After losing both that kingdom and the remnants of Tamerlane's capital at Samarkand, he crossed the Hindu Kush and occupied Kabul. The enemy of both Shaibani Khan and Ibrahim Lodi, the emperor of Delhi, he allied with Hussain Mirz of Herat and won his empire at the Battle of Panipat. For 10 points—name this father of Humayun and grandfather of Akbar who founded India's Mughal empire.

Because of his opposition to the Vietnam War, he was twice denied his seat in the Georgia state legislature until the Supreme Court intervened. In 1968, he chaired a "challenge delegation" to the Democratic National Convention. He was the convention's first choice for Vice-President, but he had to decline the nomination due to his age. For 10 points—name this founder of the Atlanta branch of the Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee who, in February 1998, was elected chairman of the NAACP.

He defeated King Aistulf's army of Lombards in a victory at Pavia, thus protecting Pope Stephen II. He then gave Ravenna and other lands to the Church, forming the Papal States, in his namesake "donation." After he deposed Childeric III, received Neustria from his brother, and conquered Aquitaine, he became the ruler of all Frankish territory. For 10 points—name this man who succeeded his father Charles Martel as mayor of the Austrasian palace and left his own lands to his sons Carloman II and Charlemagne.

To obtain water from this desert, the town of Cgungungo uses a renowned system of plastic sheets to capture fog. A leading source of sodium nitrate and copper, it lies two thousand feet above sea level and is over seven hundred miles long. Flanked by the Pacific Coastal Range and the Andes, it is considered the driest hot desert on earth. For 10 points—name this desert in Peru, Argentina, and Chile.

According to superstring theory, which mathematically requires their existence, they are closed strings with the least possible energy. Their lack of energy explains why these spin-two bosons are nearly impossible to detect. For 10 points—name these theoretical fundamental particles that carry the force which attracts two particles as a function of mass.

It was planned with the assistance of the Quaker activist Reginald Reynolds and announced in a letter to Lord Irwin. In disobedience of an 1882 monopoly act, seventy-eight volunteers from Ashram began it on March 12 in Ahmedabad. Christians and Muslims joined at Bareja and it concluded on April 6, two hundred miles to the west, in Dandi. For 10 points—name this 1930 tax protest which ended with a symbolic touching of the namesake seasoning by Mohandas Ghandi.

John Warne was a financier and barbed wire manufacturer known as "bet-a-million" for his conjectures about the stock market. Thomas led a party that was shipwrecked in Bermuda on the way to colonizing Jamestown. Henry Louis maintains a large collection of Africana as a professor at Harvard. Horatio lost at Camden but won at Saratoga. For 10 points—all share what surname with art collector, AIDS activist, Altair-BASIC author, and richest man alive Bill?

Before its 1849 discovery by Austin Layard, it was considered a Biblical myth. It displaced Calah as a capital, but it was destroyed by a coalition of Babylonians, Medes, and Scythians in 612 BCE. Its sites included the grand palace of Sennacherib and the twenty thousand cuneiform tablets found in the library of Ashurbanipal. For 10 points—name this city on the Tigris which served as the capital of the Assyrian Empire.

His second novel, When She Was Good, failed to recapture the success he obtained with Letting Go. His other novels include My Life as a Man and The Great American Novel, which were followed up by 1979's The Ghost Writer, introducing his reoccurring character Nathan Zuckerman. For 10 points—name this American author of Goodbye, Columbus, who also wrote American Pastoral and Portnoy's Complaint.

This country's head of state has received patents for a water mill, an oxygen pump and palm oil vehicle fuel. King Bhumibol Adulyadej, who is also an award-winning yacht racer and prolific musician, recently received his fourth patent, on the "super-sandwich" technique to induce rain. For 10 points—name this country known as the "land of the free" because it was never an occupied colony, formerly called Siam.

This graduate of Columbia Law School ran unsuccessfully for the U.S. House as a Republican in 1974, and he later worked as a staffer for Jesse Helms and David Duke. He was shot by a sniper during the March Against Fear, and he wrote a book about his most famous experience, a standoff with Ross Barnett. For 10 points—name this man who transferred from Jackson State College in 1961, becoming the first African-American to attend the University of Mississippi.

His San Giovenale Triptych was one of the earliest fifteenth- century works to have no Gothic influence, and he developed many of the techniques for showing light sources in such works as the Santa Maria Novella Trinity and the Pisa Altarpiece. Because he refused to devote attention to anything outside of his work, including his clothes, he was nicknamed with a term meaning "pigpen." For 10 points—name this Florentine painter of The Expulsion from Paradise and The Tribute Money.

The p450 variety plays a large role in metabolizing drugs in the liver, and genetic differences in it cause severe drug interaction problems. The c variety is a terminal electron acceptor, and like other varieties, it contains a heme group and translocates protons, helping set up a proton gradient that causes ATPase to synthesize ATP. For 10 points—name these membrane bound proteins found in the mitochondrial cristae, which play a key role in the electron transport chain.

Samuel Flagg Bemis won a Pulitzer in history for a 1927 book on this agreement. It opened the Mississippi beyond the boundaries of the Treaty of Paris, established tax-free deposit access in New Orleans, and set 31 degrees north latitude as the southern boundary of the United States. For 10 points—name this October 1795 treaty which briefly ended contention with Spain.

He made the career of Johann Gottlieb Fichte by publishing the latter's Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation. In 1770, he claimed that the works of David Hume "awoke [him] from [his] dogmatic slumber." He went on to explain "the starry heavens above…and the moral law within…" in such works as The Metaphysics of Morals. For 10 points—name this German transcendentalist who posited the categorical imperative in Critique of Judgment and Critique of Pure Reason.

He played the flügelhorn to record "Springville" and "Blues for Pablo" under the direction of Gil Evans. You're Under Arrest and Aura are among his late albums. His early efforts were released as The Birth of the Cool, which indeed created the "cool jazz" style which supplanted bebop. What is probably his most respected work was recorded with Jimmy Cobb, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, and John Coltrane among others. For 10 points—name this composer and trumpet player on Kind of Blue.

She gave up the teaching of philosophy after the 1943 publication of her first novel, She Came to Stay. Her autobiographical volumes include Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter and A Very Easy Death. She wrote about many of her relationships, for example, Nelson Algren in Les Mandarins. For 10 points—name this author of the feminist work The Second Sex and close companion of Jean-Paul Sartre.

The expansionism of August II of Poland and Danish agitation in Holstein-Gottorp began this war, which transferred Estonia and Livonia after the battles of Hangö, Narva, and Poltava. Hegemony over the gulfs of Finland and Bothnia as well as the Baltic lands began for Russia under the terms of the Treaty of Rystad. For 10 points—name this war fought from 1700 to 1721 by Charles XII of Sweden and Peter the Great.

It began with the formation of the Sat-Cho Alliance, who sought to challenge the bakufu. Developments included the granting of rights to the eta, the signing of the Charter Oath, the issuance of the Constitution of 1889, the removal of feudal authorities from the daimyo, and the start of modern industry. For 10 points—name this period of "Enlightened Rule" that saw the end of the Tokugawa Shogunate in Japan.

May 24, 1738, is celebrated as the date of his epiphany at a prayer meeting at Aldersgate Street in London, when Luther's preface to the commentary of Paul's letter to the Romans was read. Afterwards, he would shock the church hierarchy proclaiming that the world was his parish and split his denomination over the question of predestination. For 10 points—name this founder of Methodism.

The "Barbara" version is the most common example and is found in the Prior Analytics. The "Cesare" is an example of revising an "imperfect" one into a "perfect" one. Called the foundation of formal deductive reasoning, a famous one proves that Socrates is mortal. For 10 points—name this technique of Aristotelian logic which uses two premises to prove a conclusion.

Though it was established by Rule 22 in 1917, Henry Clay proposed it as early as 1841 in response to the Democrats' efforts to block the passage of his bank bill. First invoked in 1919 during the Senate debate over the Treaty of Versailles, it was revised in 1975 to have a sixty vote requirement instead of a sixty-seven vote one. For 10 points—name this Senate rule that can be used to override a filibuster and bring a bill to a vote.

Commonly used in depth-first searching algorithms and pushdown automata, this data structure is almost universally used to store information about function nesting. It also comes in handy when using reverse polish notation, as any character that is read can be compared to the symbol at the top of this data structure; if there is a match, the symbol can be removed. For 10 points—name this last-in-first out data structure, from which an object can be popped or onto which an object may be pushed.

This result holds for any pair of incompatible observables, since the commutator of the corresponding operators is non-zero. It was introduced in a paper on the interpretation of matrix mechanics which included a thought experiment with a gamma-ray microscope. Part of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, it weakens causality since perfect information is impossible. For 10 points—name this principle stating the a subatomic particle's position and momentum cannot be simultaneously and precisely known.

In 1987, he served fifty days in prison for two muggings. He released his first album, Music for the People, after his older brother got him a recording contract. A scandal over homophobic comments hurt his second album, You Gotta Believe, so he turned to acting and drew notice for roles in Fear and The Basketball Diaries. For 10 points—name this star of the remake of Planet of the Apes and The Italian Job.

Its website features clips from the show, divided into sections such as "Tell All" and "Play of the Day." Animated characters such as Sarcastic Sid and Obvious Guy make frequent appearances and comment on the two contestants, who more often than not decide never to see each other again. For 10 points—name this syndicated show hosted by Roger Lodge, which takes two people who have never met before and sends them on a namesake outing.

A demo made with the Swizz Beatz production team led to her being signed to Aftermath Entertainment, and her debut album contained the hit song "Gotta Man." Her film debut came in 2002 when she played Terri Jones in Barbershop and she followed that up later that year with a role in XXX. She won the first Grammy for Rap/Sung collaboration for a track from her album Scorpion with Gwen Stefani. For 10 points—this is what rapper also known for her song "Gangsta Love" with Alicia Keys?

Universal Waite, Rider-Waite, Robin Wood, and Morgan-Greer are standard for novices. While the artistry on each card may differ, the meanings behind each in the Major Arcana and Minor Arcana remain the same. For 10 points—name this mystic tradition of gaining insight into one's life through reading an arrangement of cards.

He stands about six-foot-four. All the downtown ladies call him "Treetop Lover," and the men just call him, "Sir." His troubles begin, however, when he ogles Doris, the wife of a jealous man. He gets into a fight with her husband, and ends up looking like a jigsaw puzzle with a couple of pieces gone. For 10 points—name this denizen of the south side of Chicago, who is badder than Old King Kong and meaner than a junkyard dog, according to Jim Croce.

Its name is derived from the Arabic for "soaked bread." An Andalusian version of it is based mostly on almonds and grapes, but it is most commonly based on an ingredient brought from the New World to Spain, where it is classified as a salad. For 10 points—identify this Spanish dish, often identified as a soup, usually based on tomatoes, and always served cold.
